describe.submission: a directory; see readme for its required contents
describe.readme:
# Shakespeare

Predict the next character in Shakespeare's writing. The evaluator checks your model on held-out text. The score is bits per character; lower is better.

**First run:** choose **Climb on AutoLab**. The starter runs on CPU. Official scoring needs private evaluation data that is omitted from the public local download.

![Write like the Bard, one character at a time](assets/hero.svg)

## Run the starter

The starter in `examples/baseline/` counts how often each character appears in
the allowed training text. It ignores the preceding text, so it is a simple
starting point rather than a strong language model. At the default settings it
scores about **4.80666995 bpc**.

On AutoLab, click **Start a climb**, then **Climb on AutoLab**. Choose an agent
model and either a connected CPU machine or **CPU only (small)**. Set a model
budget under **More options**. AutoLab copies `model.py` and `counts.json` into
the climb, so the starter can run without finding files outside its folder.
Read the baseline result before reviewing changes. Pause the climb to stop.

The starter and evaluator use only Python's standard library. Python 3.11 or
newer is required, and no GPU is needed for this first run. Training a different
model may need additional tools or compute.

## Compute and cost

The agent model writes experiments; the compute runs them. The model budget covers model calls. Rented compute is billed separately. Pause the climb to stop experiments and release AutoLab rentals; your own connected machine remains yours to manage.

Before changing anything, open the baseline job and check for a passing score. **Nodes offline** means compute is disconnected, not that your solution failed.

## Try a first change

On AutoLab, ask the agent to make this edit in your submission, then run one evaluation against the baseline.

In `model.py`, change `_SMOOTHING = 1.0` to `_SMOOTHING = 0.5`. Keep the counts
unchanged and evaluate once more. Smoothing gives a little extra probability to
rare characters. This is a small experiment in reading a score change; it does
not teach the model to use context. At the default settings this edit scores
about **4.80666742 bpc**, a very small improvement.

Next, try a **bigram model**: count which characters follow each character in
`train.txt`, then use the last character of the prefix to choose a distribution.
Keep smoothing so unseen pairs still receive probability. Compare with your
baseline using the same evaluation settings.

## What to submit

Submit a directory containing `model.py` with this function:

```python
predict_next(prefix: str) -> dict[str, float]
```

Return a dict mapping each candidate character to its **natural-log probability**.
For example, probability `0.5` is written as `math.log(0.5)`, about `-0.6931`,
not as `0.5`. Returned values must be finite and no greater than zero; the
probabilities must add up to at most one. Missing characters receive the floor
penalty rather than a free pass.

The evaluator calls the function with the text seen so far: first an empty
prefix, then one character more on each call. It never passes the next character
as an argument. You can keep incremental state to avoid rescanning the prefix.

You may change the model, train offline, and ship learned tables or weights.
Model inference must use only Python's standard library. Load packaged assets
relative to `model.py`, as the starter does with `counts.json`.

## Training data and local work

The first 90% of the corpus is the public `train.txt` in this hill. Use only that
text for training. The starter's packaged counts were computed from it. Keep
any new training code and model assets in your own workspace, leaving the hill's
evaluator and data unchanged.

**Use AutoLab for scored runs with the public version.** The public download
omits `private/val.txt`, which official scoring requires. You can develop a model
locally using `train.txt`, but that download alone cannot run the official
evaluation. A separate public practice evaluation is not provided yet.

If you have an authorized complete hill bundle, the local starter command is:

```sh
cp -R .autolab/hills/shakespeare/examples/baseline ./my-model
hills eval ./my-model -H shakespeare -o baseline.json
```

Run this from the project folder containing `.autolab/`, using a fresh `my-model`
folder. Local results are not automatically added to AutoLab's leaderboard.

## How scoring works

The evaluator measures the average negative log probability assigned to the
characters that actually occur, converted to base two. The metric is **`bpc`**;
lower is better. A missing or zero-probability character is scored with a floor
of `1e-8`. The result includes `details.chars_scored`.

Invalid distributions fail with an explanation in `details.error`. A valid
model can still score badly: always predicting one character confidently does
not make its other predictions correct.

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `eval_chars` | 8000 | Maximum held-out characters scored per run |

Use the same character count when comparing attempts. `--final` scores a
different half of the held-out text and records a separate comparison group.
Keep reports unedited; `hills verify` checks their signatures with the matching
signing key.

## Trust

This is a cooperative learning exercise. Train only on `train.txt`; do not read
or reconstruct held-out text from elsewhere. The evaluator checks the prediction
interface and distributions, but it is not an isolation boundary: on AutoLab,
submission code and evaluation currently run as the same operating-system user.

## If the first run fails

- **Missing held-out data on your laptop:** the public download cannot run official scoring. Use **Climb on AutoLab**; do not try to obtain or recreate the private text.
- **Missing `counts.json`:** copy the whole starter folder, not just `model.py`.
- **Invalid probabilities:** return natural-log probabilities. For probability 0.5, use `math.log(0.5)`; check that the probabilities sum to at most one.

The score is in bits per character even though the function returns natural logs. Compare the same `eval_chars` and evaluation mode; lower is better.

## Versions and comparisons

A climb stays on the hill version selected when it was created. To try a newly published version, start a new climb from the hill page. Old results stay with their original version, including when a new version only changes this README.

spec_version: 2
name: shakespeare
version: 0.1.0

# Model inference on a CPU slice of the validation split; generous cap for
# slow pure-python models.
watchdog_timeout_s: 900

metrics:
  - {name: bpc, direction: min}

params:
  eval_chars: {type: int, default: 8000, min: 1000, max: 55000}
